claim: A novel FMNL1 knock-out mouse model was developed by inserting a LacZ-neomycin cassette into the Fmnl1 locus of C57BL/6 mice.
source: To determine the role of FMNL1 in immune cell function, we generated FMNL1 KO mice by inserting a LacZ-neomycin cassette into the Fmnl1 locus of C57BL/6 mice (Figure 1A).
evidence: The manuscript describes the generation method and provides a schematic in Figure 1A showing the targeting construct.

claim: The correct insertion of the LacZ-neomycin cassette was confirmed via PCR.
source: We confirmed the correct insertion of this cassette via PCR (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) and verified deletion of FMNL1 at the protein level via western blot (Figure 1B).
evidence: PCR results are shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 confirming the insertion.

claim: FMNL1 protein expression is completely lost in T cells from mice homozygous for the Fmnl1 KO allele.
source: We confirmed the correct insertion of this cassette via PCR (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) and verified deletion of FMNL1 at the protein level via western blot (Figure 1B).
evidence: Western blot in Figure 1B shows complete loss of FMNL1 protein in KO mice.

claim: FMNL1 deficiency does not alter the number and frequency of major immune cell populations in the thymus, blood, and secondary lymphoid organs.
source: Flow cytometric analysis of the blood and primary and secondary lymphoid organs revealed no major differences in the number and proportions of either lymphoid (Figure 1—figure supplement 2) or myeloid populations (Figure 1—figure supplement 3) between FMNL1 KO and age matched control mice.
evidence: Flow cytometry data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2 and 3 show no significant differences in immune cell populations.

claim: Activated FMNL1 KO T cells displayed a 3.8-fold average reduction in trafficking to the pancreatic islets compared to control T cells.
source: Activated FMNL1 KO T cells displayed a 3.8-fold average reduction in trafficking to the islets compared to control T cells. (Figure 2B,C).
evidence: Quantification of trafficking shown in Figure 2B demonstrates reduced islet trafficking.

claim: 100% of mice receiving control T cells developed diabetes, while only 44% of mice receiving FMNL1 KO T cells developed diabetes in the RIP-mOVA model.
source: While 100% of mice receiving control T cells developed diabetes, only 44% of mice receiving FMNL1 KO T cells developed diabetes (Figure 2E).
evidence: Diabetes incidence data shown in Figure 2E demonstrates protection from disease.

claim: FMNL1 KO T cells proliferate equivalently to WT T cells in response to CD3 stimulus.
source: We found no major differences in the proliferation, the expression of canonical markers of activation and chemokine receptors, or the size of FMNL1 KO T cells compared to WT T cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Figure 2—figure supplement 1A shows equivalent proliferation of WT and FMNL1 KO T cells.

claim: CD3 activated WT and FMNL1 KO T cells express equivalent levels of adhesion molecules and activation markers.
source: We found no major differences in the proliferation, the expression of canonical markers of activation and chemokine receptors, or the size of FMNL1 KO T cells compared to WT T cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Figure 2—figure supplement 1B shows equivalent expression of adhesion molecules and activation markers.

claim: Activated FMNL1 KO T cells had a 1.4-fold reduction in trafficking to the brain and a 2.2-fold reduction in trafficking to the spinal cord compared to control T cells in the EAE model.
source: Activated FMNL1 KO T cells had a 1.4-fold reduction in trafficking to the brain and a 2.2-fold reduction in trafficking to the spinal cord compared to control T cells (Figure 3B,C).
evidence: Quantification of CNS trafficking shown in Figure 3B demonstrates reduced trafficking to brain and spinal cord.

claim: 100% of mice receiving control 2D2 T cells developed EAE, while only 33% of mice receiving FMNL1 KO 2D2 T cells developed EAE.
source: While 100% of mice receiving control 2D2 T cells developed EAE, only 33% of mice receiving FMNL1 KO 2D2 T cells developed EAE (Figure 3E).
evidence: EAE incidence data shown in Figure 3E demonstrates protection from disease.

claim: Mice receiving control T cells displayed an average peak disease score of 3.5 compared to an average peak score of 0.67 for mice receiving FMNL1 KO T cells in the EAE model.
source: Mice receiving control T cells displayed an average peak disease score of 3.5 compared to an average peak score of 0.67 for mice receiving FMNL1 KO T cells (Figure 3E).
evidence: EAE disease score data shown in Figure 3E demonstrates reduced disease severity.

claim: Naive FMNL1 KO T cells traffic equivalently to WT T cells to secondary lymphoid organs under homeostatic conditions.
source: Twenty-four hours post- intravenous transfer, we found equivalent ratios and numbers of transferred control and FMNL1 KO naïve T cells in the spleen, lymph nodes, and blood of recipient mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B,C).
evidence: Trafficking data in Figure 3—figure supplement 2C shows no significant differences in naive T cell trafficking to lymphoid organs.

claim: FMNL1 deficiency does not affect T cell adhesion to the endothelial monolayer.
source: Quantification of the number of cells adhering to the endothelium and subsequently detaching under flow, revealed no differences between WT and FMNL1 KO T cells (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: Quantification in Figure 4C shows equivalent adhesion of WT and FMNL1 KO T cells.

claim: Both WT and FMNL1 KO T cells are equally capable of crawling on the endothelial monolayer.
source: Similarly, both WT and FMNL1 KO T cells were equally capable of crawling on the endothelial monolayer (Figure 4E), suggesting that FMNL1 is dispensable during the first stages of TEM.
evidence: Quantification in Figure 4E shows equivalent crawling behavior.

claim: FMNL1 KO T cells are equivalent to WT cells in their ability to initiate diapedesis.
source: While FMNL1 KO T cells were equivalent to WT cells in their ability to initiate diapedesis (Figure 4F), they had a 3.8-fold reduction in their ability to complete the TEM process (Figure 4G).
evidence: Quantification in Figure 4F shows equivalent initiation of diapedesis.

claim: FMNL1 KO T cells had a 3.8-fold reduction in their ability to complete the TEM process.
source: While FMNL1 KO T cells were equivalent to WT cells in their ability to initiate diapedesis (Figure 4F), they had a 3.8-fold reduction in their ability to complete the TEM process (Figure 4G).
evidence: Quantification in Figure 4G shows reduced completion of TEM.

claim: FMNL1 KO T cells that complete TEM take more than twice as long on average compared to WT T cells.
source: Furthermore, the few FMNL1 KO T cells that were able to complete TEM took more than twice as long on average compared to WT T cells (Figure 4H).
evidence: Quantification in Figure 4H shows prolonged TEM duration for FMNL1 KO T cells.

claim: FMNL1 is enriched behind the nucleus in 64% of transmigrating WT T cells, with an additional 12.5% displaying partial perinuclear enrichment.
source: On average we found posterior perinuclear enrichment of FMNL1 in 64% of transmigrating WT T cells, with an additional 12.5% displaying a partial perinuclear enrichment (Figure 5D).
evidence: Quantification in Figure 5D shows perinuclear FMNL1 enrichment in transmigrating T cells.

claim: FMNL1 KO T cells are significantly impaired in their ability to transmigrate their nuclei, with only 7% of transmigrating T cells having migrated their nuclei below the endothelium compared to 32% for WT T cells.
source: FMNL1 KO T cells were significantly impaired in their ability to transmigrate their nuclei, with only 7% of transmigrating T cells having migrated their nuclei below the endothelium compared to 32% for WT T cells (Figure 5E).
evidence: Quantification in Figure 5E shows impaired nuclear transmigration in FMNL1 KO T cells.

claim: Activated FMNL1 KO cells are impaired in their ability to migrate across 3 μm transwell inserts compared to activated WT T cells in response to CXCL12.
source: In response to CXCL12, activated FMNL1 KO cells were impaired in their ability to migrate across 3 μm transwell inserts compared to activated WT T cells (Figure 6A).
evidence: Transwell migration data in Figure 6A shows impaired migration through 3 μm pores.

claim: FMNL1 KO cells migrate to CXCL12 equivalently as WT T cells across 5 μm transwell inserts.
source: However, FMNL1 KO cells migrated to CXCL12 equivalently as WT T cells across 5 μm transwell inserts (Figure 6A).
evidence: Transwell migration data in Figure 6A shows equivalent migration through 5 μm pores.

claim: In response to CXCL10, FMNL1 KO T cells are impaired in migrating across 3 μm, but not 5 μm transwell inserts.
source: This effect was not exclusive to CXCL12, in fact in response to CXCL10, FMNL1 KO T cells were similarly impaired in migrating across 3 μm, but not 5 μm transwell inserts (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Transwell migration data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A shows pore size-dependent migration defect with CXCL10.

claim: FMNL1 KO neutrophils display equivalent migration compared to WT neutrophils in response to CXCL1 through 3 μm transwell pores.
source: In response to the neutrophil chemoattractant CXCL1, FMNL1 KO neutrophils displayed equivalent migration compared to WT neutrophils (Figure 6B).
evidence: Neutrophil transwell migration data in Figure 6B shows no impairment in FMNL1 KO neutrophils.

claim: Unstimulated WT and FMNL1 KO T cells display similar baseline levels of F-actin.
source: Unstimulated WT and FMNL1 KO T cells displayed similar baseline levels of F-actin (Figure 6C).
evidence: F-actin quantification in Figure 6C shows equivalent baseline levels.

claim: In response to 15 s of CXCL12 stimulus, WT T cells increase their total polymerized actin an average of 1.8 fold, while FMNL1 KO T cells only increase their total polymerized actin an average of 1.4 fold.
source: In response to 15 s of CXCL12 stimulus, WT T cells increased their total polymerized actin an average of 1.8 fold, while FMNL1 KO T cell only increased their total polymerized actin an average of 1.4 fold (Figure 6D).
evidence: Actin polymerization data in Figure 6D shows reduced response to CXCL12 in FMNL1 KO T cells.

claim: FMNL1 KO T cells display impaired actin polymerization in response to CXCL10 stimulus.
source: We also observed a similar impairment in FMNL1 KO T cell actin polymerization in response to CXCL10 stimulus (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Actin polymerization data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B shows reduced response to CXCL10.

claim: Re-expression of FMNL1 in FMNL1 KO T cells restores their ability to transmigrate through 3 μm pores.
source: However, re-expression of FMNL1 in FMNL1 KO T cells restored their ability to transmigrate through the 3 μm pores (Figure 6E).
evidence: Transwell migration data in Figure 6E shows rescue of migration defect by FMNL1 re-expression.

claim: There is a strong positive correlation between the level of FMNL1 expressed by a given population of T cells and their ability to transmigrate through restrictive pores.
source: We found a strong positive correlation between the level of FMNL1 expressed by a given population of T cells and their ability to transmigrate through restrictive pores (Figure 6F).
evidence: Correlation analysis in Figure 6F shows positive correlation between FMNL1 expression and migration.

claim: FMNL1-deficient T cells are significantly impaired in migrating through 3 µm constriction points in microchannels.
source: Using this system, we imaged control and FMNL1 KO T cell migration within these microchannels and found that, similar to our transwell system results, FMNL1-deficient T cells were significantly impaired in migrating through the 3 µm constriction points in the microchannels (Figure 7B).
evidence: Microchannel migration data in Figure 7B shows impaired passage through constrictions.

claim: Control T cells enrich their F-actin content around the back of the nucleus when it has to deform upon encountering a constriction.
source: Our analysis shows that control T cells enrich their F-actin content around the back of the nucleus when it has to deform upon encountering a constriction. However, FMNL1-deficient T cells were impaired in their ability to generate this posterior perinuclear F-actin enrichment when encountering a constriction (Figure 7D and E).
evidence: F-actin distribution analysis in Figure 7D and E shows posterior perinuclear enrichment in control T cells during constriction.

claim: FMNL1-deficient T cells are impaired in their ability to generate posterior perinuclear F-actin enrichment when encountering a constriction.
source: Our analysis shows that control T cells enrich their F-actin content around the back of the nucleus when it has to deform upon encountering a constriction. However, FMNL1-deficient T cells were impaired in their ability to generate this posterior perinuclear F-actin enrichment when encountering a constriction (Figure 7D and E).
evidence: F-actin distribution analysis in Figure 7D and E shows lack of posterior perinuclear enrichment in FMNL1 KO T cells during constriction.

claim: FMNL1 is selectively required for effector T cell trafficking to inflamed tissues, without affecting naïve T cell entry into secondary lymphoid organs.
source: We developed a new Formin-like-1 (FMNL1) knock-out mouse model and determined that the cytoskeletal effector FMNL1 is selectively required for effector T cell trafficking to inflamed tissues, without affecting naïve T cell entry into secondary lymphoid organs.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by trafficking data in Figures 2, 3, and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: FMNL1 mediates a mechanism of actin polymerization at the back of the cell that enables migration of the rigid lymphocyte nucleus through restrictive barriers.
source: Here, we identify a FMNL1-dependent mechanism of actin polymerization at the back of the cell that enables migration of the rigid lymphocyte nucleus through restrictive barriers.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figures 5, 6, and 7.

claim: FMNL1-deficiency impairs the ability of self-reactive effector T cells to induce autoimmune disease.
source: Furthermore, FMNL1-deficiency impairs the ability of self-reactive effector T cells to induce autoimmune disease.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by disease data in Figures 2E and 3E.

claim: FMNL1 may be a potential therapeutic target to specifically modulate T cell trafficking to inflammatory sites.
source: Overall, our data suggest that FMNL1 may be a potential therapeutic target to specifically modulate T cell trafficking to inflammatory sites.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings showing selective impairment of effector T cell trafficking and autoimmune disease.

claim: T cell trafficking and extravasation into tissues are required for proper immune surveillance and execution of effector functions against pathogens and malignant cells.
source: T cell trafficking and extravasation into tissues are required for proper immune surveillance and execution of effector functions against pathogens and malignant cells (Masopust and Schenkel, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Masopust and Schenkel, 2013.

claim: In the context of aberrant immune function, T cell entry into target tissues can be a driver of autoimmune and inflammatory diseases.
source: However, in the context of aberrant immune function, T cell entry into target tissues can be a driver of autoimmune and inflammatory diseases (Sallusto et al., 2012; Magnuson et al., 2015; Mellado et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Sallusto et al., 2012; Magnuson et al., 2015; Mellado et al., 2015.

claim: Disruption of T cell trafficking by targeting integrins or chemotactic stimuli appears to be a promising approach to achieving immune regulation in some disease contexts.
source: Indeed, disruption of T cell trafficking by targeting integrins or chemotactic stimuli appears to be a promising approach to achieving immune regulation in some disease contexts (Engelhardt and Kappos, 2008; Luster et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Engelhardt and Kappos, 2008; Luster et al., 2005.

claim: Many of the adhesion molecules and chemokines that orchestrate T cell trafficking have been well characterized.
source: Many of the adhesion molecules and chemokines that orchestrate T cell trafficking have been well characterized (Nourshargh and Alon, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Nourshargh and Alon, 2014.

claim: Less is known about downstream effectors that directly mediate the cytoskeletal changes necessary to elicit the force generation and shape changes inherent to the migratory process and entry into tissues.
source: However, less is known about downstream effectors that directly mediate the cytoskeletal changes necessary to elicit the force generation and shape changes inherent to the migratory process and entry into tissues.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field.

claim: T cells undergo the multistep process of transendothelial migration (TEM) to exit blood vessels and enter tissues.
source: To exit blood vessels and enter tissues, T cells undergo the multistep process of transendothelial migration (TEM).
evidence: This is established knowledge about T cell migration.

claim: T cells are initially captured from the blood flow to begin selectin-mediated rolling along the vascular endothelial wall, followed by firm adherence in a chemokine driven integrin-mediated process.
source: T cells are initially captured from the blood flow to begin selectin-mediated rolling along the vascular endothelial wall, followed by firm adherence in a chemokine driven integrin-mediated process.
evidence: This describes the established steps of TEM.

claim: After crawling along the endothelium probing for permissive sites for extravasation, T cells initiate the diapedesis step and squeeze through the vascular endothelium.
source: After crawling along the endothelium probing for permissive sites for extravasation, T cells initiate the diapedesis step and squeeze through the vascular endothelium (Nourshargh and Alon, 2014).
evidence: This describes the established steps of TEM, supported by citation to Nourshargh and Alon, 2014.

claim: T cells rely on morphological changes and force generation mediated by remodeling of the actin cytoskeleton to undergo the stages of TEM.
source: To undergo the stages of TEM, T cells rely on morphological changes and force generation mediated by remodeling of the actin cytoskeleton (Alon and Shulman, 2011; Dupré et al., 2015; Ridley, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Alon and Shulman, 2011; Dupré et al., 2015; Ridley, 2011.

claim: Deformation of the rigid lymphocyte nucleus is a rate-limiting step for migration through confined environments such as during TEM.
source: Furthermore, deformation of the rigid lymphocyte nucleus is a rate-limiting step for migration through confined environments such as during TEM (Friedl et al., 2011; Alon and van Buul, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Friedl et al., 2011; Alon and van Buul, 2017.

claim: Actin networks in T cells consist of branched and linear filaments that are cross-linked by the motor protein non-muscle Myosin IIA (MyoIIA).
source: Actin networks in T cells consist of branched and linear filaments that are cross-linked by the motor protein non-muscle Myosin IIA (MyoIIA) (Dupré et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Dupré et al., 2015.

claim: MyoIIA mediates squeezing of the nucleus during the diapedesis step of TEM.
source: We have previously shown that MyoIIA mediates squeezing of the nucleus during the diapedesis step of TEM (Jacobelli et al., 2013; Wigton et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work by the authors (Jacobelli et al., 2013; Wigton et al., 2016).

claim: Branched actin networks, which are generated by the Arp2/3 complex and its upstream regulator WASP, play a role in T cell trafficking as well as membrane protrusion generation during TEM.
source: Branched actin networks, which are generated by the Arp2/3 complex and its upstream regulator WASP, play a role in T cell trafficking as well as membrane protrusion generation during TEM (Snapper et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Snapper et al., 2005.

claim: Linear actin polymerization is mediated by two major families in T cells: the Ena/VASP (vasodilator-stimulated phosphoprotein) family and the formin family.
source: Linear actin polymerization is mediated by two major families in T cells: the Ena/VASP (vasodilator-stimulated phosphoprotein) family and the formin family.
evidence: This is established knowledge about actin polymerization in T cells.

claim: The Ena/VASP family elongates actin filaments through anti-capping activity and recruitment of actin monomers.
source: The Ena/VASP family elongates actin filaments through anti-capping activity and recruitment of actin monomers (Chesarone and Goode, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Chesarone and Goode, 2009.

claim: Ena/VASP proteins modulate α4 integrin expression and function in T cells to promote diapedesis.
source: We have recently shown that Ena/VASP proteins modulate α4 integrin expression and function in T cells to promote diapedesis (Estin et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work by the authors (Estin et al., 2017).

claim: Formins remodel the actin cytoskeleton by both nucleating new actin filaments and processively elongating them through recruitment of profilin-bound actin monomers and protection from anti-capping proteins.
source: Formins remodel the actin cytoskeleton by both nucleating new actin filaments and processively elongating them through recruitment of profilin-bound actin monomers and protection from anti-capping proteins (Faix and Grosse, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Faix and Grosse, 2006.

claim: Two members of the formin family are highly expressed in T cells: Diaphanous-related formin-1 (mDia1, Diaph1) and Formin-like 1 (FMNL1, FRL1).
source: Two members of the formin family are highly expressed in T cells: Diaphanous-related formin-1 (mDia1, Diaph1) and Formin-like 1 (FMNL1, FRL1) (Gomez et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Gomez et al., 2007.

claim: Previous studies have identified a role for mDia1 in promoting T cell trafficking out of the thymus and into peripheral tissues.
source: Previous studies have identified a role for mDia1 in promoting T cell trafficking out of the thymus and into peripheral tissues (Sakata et al., 2007; Eisenmann et al., 2007; Vicente-Manzanares et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Sakata et al., 2007; Eisenmann et al., 2007; Vicente-Manzanares et al., 2003.

claim: mDia1 promotes completion of diapedesis in B cell leukemia.
source: While a specific role for mDia1 in T cell TEM has not been identified, we have recently shown that mDia1 promotes completion of diapedesis in B cell leukemia (Thompson et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work by the authors (Thompson et al., 2018).

claim: FMNL1 expression is largely restricted to cells of the hematopoietic lineage.
source: Unlike mDia1, which is expressed in a wide variety of cell types, FMNL1 expression is largely restricted to cells of the hematopoietic lineage (Yayoshi-Yamamoto et al., 2000; Gardberg et al., 2014; Yue et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Yayoshi-Yamamoto et al., 2000; Gardberg et al., 2014; Yue et al., 2014.

claim: FMNL1 has previously been implicated in macrophage phagocytosis, membrane protrusion formation and migration.
source: FMNL1 has previously been implicated in macrophage phagocytosis, membrane protrusion formation and migration (Miller et al., 2017; Yayoshi-Yamamoto et al., 2000; Seth et al., 2006; Naj et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Miller et al., 2017; Yayoshi-Yamamoto et al., 2000; Seth et al., 2006; Naj et al., 2013.

claim: In leukemia cells, FMNL1 has been suggested to be involved in membrane dynamics, proliferation and migration.
source: In leukemia cells, FMNL1 has been suggested to be involved in membrane dynamics, proliferation and migration (Favaro et al., 2013; Han et al., 2009; Han et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Favaro et al., 2013; Han et al., 2009; Han et al., 2013.

claim: Previous studies have suggested that FMNL1 contributes to the reorientation of the centrosome to the immune synapse and Golgi apparatus structure in Jurkat transformed T cells as well as the cytotoxic behavior of CD8 T cells.
source: Previous studies have suggested that FMNL1 contributes to the reorientation of the centrosome to the immune synapse and Golgi apparatus structure in Jurkat transformed T cells as well as the cytotoxic behavior of CD8 T cells (Gomez et al., 2007; Colón-Franco et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gomez et al., 2007; Colón-Franco et al., 2011.

claim: FMNL1 expression has been reported to be transcriptionally upregulated by T cells in autoimmune contexts.
source: Additionally, FMNL1 expression has been reported to be transcriptionally upregulated by T cells in autoimmune contexts (Odoardi et al., 2012; Degroote et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Odoardi et al., 2012; Degroote et al., 2017.

claim: The role and potential mechanism of action of FMNL1 in the motility, trafficking and TEM of primary lymphocytes is unknown.
source: However, the role and potential mechanism of action of FMNL1 in the motility, trafficking and TEM of primary lymphocytes is unknown.
evidence: This is a statement about the gap in knowledge that the study addresses.

claim: Previous studies relied on RNAi approaches or myeloid specific deletion to investigate FMNL1.
source: Since previous studies relied on RNAi approaches (Gomez et al., 2007; Seth et al., 2006; Favaro et al., 2013; Han et al., 2009; Naj et al., 2013) or myeloid specific deletion to investigate FMNL1 (Miller et al., 2017), we developed a novel germline FMNL1 knockout (KO) mouse to investigate the requirement and mechanism of action of FMNL1 in primary lymphocyte migration.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies using different approaches.

claim: A prior report suggested that complete FMNL1 deficiency in mice would be embryonically lethal.
source: A prior report suggested that complete FMNL1 deficiency in mice would be embryonically lethal (Miller et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Miller et al., 2017.

claim: FMNL1-deficient mice are viable and breed normally.
source: However, our FMNL1-deficient mice are viable and breed normally.
evidence: This is an observation from the study that contradicts the prior report.

claim: The discrepancy in embryonic lethality may be due to differences in the targeting approach and use of a ubiquitously expressed Cre recombinase in the earlier approach.
source: This discrepancy may be due to differences in the targeting approach and use of a ubiquitously expressed Cre recombinase in the earlier approach.
evidence: This is speculation about the reason for the discrepancy with the prior report.

claim: Normal populations of immune cells within the blood, spleen, and lymph nodes of FMNL1-deficient mice suggest that FMNL1 is dispensable for hematopoiesis.
source: Our observation of normal populations of immune cells within the blood, spleen, and lymph nodes of FMNL1-deficient mice suggests that FMNL1 is dispensable for hematopoiesis.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation of normal immune cell populations.

claim: Other formins, such as mDia1, likely have a more predominant role in lymphocyte development and proliferation, and/or can compensate for the loss of FMNL1.
source: It is likely that other formins, such as mDia1, have a more predominant role in lymphocyte development and proliferation, and/or can compensate for the loss of FMNL1.
evidence: This is speculation about potential compensation by other formins.

claim: The remodeling of the actin cytoskeleton is critical for morphological changes and mechanotransduction throughout the TEM process.
source: The remodeling of the actin cytoskeleton is critical for morphological changes and mechanotransduction throughout the TEM process (Dupré et al., 2015; Alon and Shulman, 2011; Ridley, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Dupré et al., 2015; Alon and Shulman, 2011; Ridley, 2011.

claim: Anchoring of integrins to the actin cytoskeleton is critical for firm adhesion and crawling upon to the endothelial monolayer.
source: Anchoring of integrins to the actin cytoskeleton is critical for firm adhesion and crawling upon to the endothelial monolayer, while the generation of actin-rich membrane protrusions is important for probing the endothelial monolayer and initiating diapedesis (Alon and Shulman, 2011; Dupré et al., 2015; Ridley, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Alon and Shulman, 2011; Dupré et al., 2015; Ridley, 2011.

claim: The generation of actin-rich membrane protrusions is important for probing the endothelial monolayer and initiating diapedesis.
source: Anchoring of integrins to the actin cytoskeleton is critical for firm adhesion and crawling upon to the endothelial monolayer, while the generation of actin-rich membrane protrusions is important for probing the endothelial monolayer and initiating diapedesis (Alon and Shulman, 2011; Dupré et al., 2015; Ridley, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Alon and Shulman, 2011; Dupré et al., 2015; Ridley, 2011.

claim: Despite displaying reduced actin polymerizing capacity in response to chemokines, FMNL1-deficient T cells were equivalent to WT cells in their ability to adhere and crawl on to the endothelial monolayer and initiate diapedesis.
source: Surprisingly, despite displaying reduced actin polymerizing capacity in response to chemokines, FMNL1-deficient T cells were equivalent to WT cells in their ability to adhere and crawl on to the endothelial monolayer and initiate diapedesis.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from Figures 4 and 6.

claim: Previous studies of macrophages reported that FMNL1 promotes the adhesion and migration of macrophages through the formation of membrane protrusions known as podosomes.
source: These observations differ from previous studies of macrophages where FMNL1 was reported to promote the adhesion and migration of macrophages through the formation of membrane protrusions known as podosomes (Miller et al., 2017; Yayoshi-Yamamoto et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Miller et al., 2017; Yayoshi-Yamamoto et al., 2000.

claim: Similar membrane structures in T cells have been suggested to play an important role in sensing of chemokine and initiating diapedesis.
source: While similar membrane structures in T cells have been suggested to play an important role in sensing of chemokine and initiating diapedesis (Dupré et al., 2015), our observations of normal crawling and diapedesis initiation in FMNL1-deficient T cells suggest that FMNL1 may not be required for these functions in T cells.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Dupré et al., 2015 and inference from the data.

claim: FMNL1 may not be required for crawling and diapedesis initiation functions in T cells.
source: While similar membrane structures in T cells have been suggested to play an important role in sensing of chemokine and initiating diapedesis (Dupré et al., 2015), our observations of normal crawling and diapedesis initiation in FMNL1-deficient T cells suggest that FMNL1 may not be required for these functions in T cells.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that FMNL1 KO T cells have normal crawling and diapedesis initiation.

claim: The cellular localization of FMNL1 appears different between macrophages and T cells, with FMNL1 enriched in ventral podosomal structures in macrophages but enriched behind the nucleus in T cells during TEM.
source: The cellular localization of FMNL1 also appears different between macrophages and T cells, with FMNL1 enriched in ventral podosomal structures in macrophages (Miller et al., 2017) but enriched behind the nucleus in T cells during TEM as shown herein.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Miller et al., 2017 for macrophages and data in Figure 5 for T cells.

claim: These observations argue for a distinct or additional role for FMNL1 in T cells compared to macrophages.
source: These observations argue for a distinct or additional role for FMNL1 in T cells compared to macrophages.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the differences in FMNL1 function and localization between T cells and macrophages.

claim: Completion of diapedesis relies on actin remodeling and force generation.
source: Completion of diapedesis also relies on actin remodeling and force generation as our previous work with the actin polymerizing Ena/VASP proteins and the cytoskeletal motor protein MyoIIA has demonstrated (Jacobelli et al., 2013; Estin et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work by the authors (Jacobelli et al., 2013; Estin et al., 2017).

claim: Similar to Ena/VASP proteins, FMNL1 is dispensable for the early stages of T cell TEM, instead being required for efficient completion of diapedesis.
source: Similar to Ena/VASP proteins, FMNL1 is dispensable for the early stages of T cell TEM, instead being required for efficient completion of diapedesis.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from Figure 4.

claim: FMNL1, like Ena/VASP proteins, has a selective role in the trafficking of activated cells.
source: Our data also suggest that FMNL1, like Ena/VASP proteins, has a selective role in the trafficking of activated cells.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the trafficking data showing selective impairment in activated T cells.

claim: Despite both Ena/VASP proteins and FMNL1 being propagators of linear actin filaments, they appear to have distinct mechanisms of action.
source: Despite both Ena/VASP proteins and FMNL1 being propagators of linear actin filaments, they appear to have distinct mechanisms of action.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the different effects of Ena/VASP and FMNL1 deficiency.

claim: Ena/VASP proteins mediate diapedesis through regulating the expression and function of α4 integrin.
source: Whereas Ena/VASP proteins mediate diapedesis through regulating the expression and function of α4 integrin (Estin et al., 2017), our data suggest that FMNL1 mediates diapedesis by promoting transmigration of the nucleus.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work by the authors (Estin et al., 2017).

claim: FMNL1 mediates diapedesis by promoting transmigration of the nucleus.
source: Whereas Ena/VASP proteins mediate diapedesis through regulating the expression and function of α4 integrin (Estin et al., 2017), our data suggest that FMNL1 mediates diapedesis by promoting transmigration of the nucleus.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 5 showing impaired nuclear transmigration in FMNL1 KO T cells.

claim: Ena/VASP deficiency impairs the trafficking of activated T cells to both lymphoid tissue and inflammatory sites, where α4 integrin can be involved.
source: Thus, while Ena/VASP deficiency impairs the trafficking of activated T cells to both lymphoid tissue and inflammatory sites, where α4 integrin can be involved (Issekutz, 1991), FMNL1 deficiency only impairs trafficking to non-lymphoid tissue sites with more restrictive endothelial barriers.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Issekutz, 1991 and comparison with FMNL1 data.

claim: FMNL1 deficiency only impairs trafficking to non-lymphoid tissue sites with more restrictive endothelial barriers.
source: Thus, while Ena/VASP deficiency impairs the trafficking of activated T cells to both lymphoid tissue and inflammatory sites, where α4 integrin can be involved (Issekutz, 1991), FMNL1 deficiency only impairs trafficking to non-lymphoid tissue sites with more restrictive endothelial barriers.
evidence: This is supported by trafficking data in Figures 2, 3, and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The nature of the vascular bed through which T cells transmigrate modulates the requirement for FMNL1.
source: These observations suggest that the nature of the vascular bed through which T cells transmigrate modulates the requirement for FMNL1 and can, in part, explain why FMNL1-deficiency affects effector T cells but not naïve T cells.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the differential effects of FMNL1 deficiency on trafficking to different tissues.

claim: Endothelial vascular barriers such as in HEVs in lymph nodes are more permissive compared to vascular barriers in peripheral tissues, which form more complex and restrictive tight junctions.
source: Endothelial vascular barriers such as in HEVs in lymph nodes are more permissive compared to vascular barriers in peripheral tissues, which form more complex and restrictive tight junctions.
evidence: This is established knowledge about differences in vascular barriers.

claim: The barrier difference between lymphoid and non-lymphoid tissues likely requires additional force generation by the T cell to push its rigid nucleus through these restrictive barriers, a process that more heavily relies on FMNL1.
source: This barrier difference likely requires additional force generation by the T cell to push its rigid nucleus through these restrictive barriers, a process that more heavily relies on FMNL1.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the data showing FMNL1-dependent nuclear transmigration and pore size-dependent migration.

claim: The finding that FMNL1 is involved in promoting the transmigration of the rigid nucleus during migration through restrictive barriers is supported by transwell and microchannel migration data, in which the role for FMNL1 appears to be pore size dependent.
source: This finding is supported by our transwell and microchannel migration data, in which the role for FMNL1 appears to be pore size dependent, consistent with the idea that FMNL1 is involved in promoting the transmigration of the rigid nucleus during migration through restrictive barriers.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figures 6 and 7 showing pore size-dependent migration defects.

claim: MyoIIA facilitates nuclear transmigration in T cells, providing contractile force to deform the rigid nuclear structure during both TEM and in migration through restrictive environments.
source: MyoIIA has also been reported to facilitate nuclear transmigration in T cells, providing contractile force to deform the rigid nuclear structure during both TEM and in migration through restrictive environments (Jacobelli et al., 2013; Friedl et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Jacobelli et al., 2013; Friedl et al., 2011.

claim: FMNL1 displays a perinuclear localization during TEM similar to MyoIIA.
source: FMNL1 displays a perinuclear localization during TEM similar to MyoIIA, and we identified a role for FMNL1 in generating perinuclear actin structures during migration under confinement.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 5 showing FMNL1 localization and Figure 7 showing perinuclear actin structures.

claim: FMNL1-deficient T cells have impaired nuclear transmigration and completion of diapedesis, analogous to MyoIIA-deficient T cells.
source: Analogous to MyoIIA-deficient T cells, FMNL1-deficient T cells also have impaired nuclear transmigration and completion of diapedesis.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figures 4 and 5 and comparison with previous MyoIIA studies.

claim: FMNL1 may be acting either in parallel or in cooperation with MyoIIA to facilitate nuclear transmigration.
source: Thus, FMNL1 may be acting either in parallel or in cooperation with MyoIIA to facilitate nuclear transmigration.
evidence: This is speculation about the relationship between FMNL1 and MyoIIA.

claim: One possibility is that FMNL1 is generating an actin network that is then crosslinked by MyoIIA to generate contractile force.
source: One possibility is that FMNL1 is generating an actin network that is then crosslinked by MyoIIA to generate contractile force.
evidence: This is speculation about a potential mechanism.

claim: Alternatively, FMNL1 may be generating different actin structures to provide propulsion force for nuclear transmigration.
source: Alternatively, FMNL1 may be generating different actin structures to provide propulsion force for nuclear transmigration.
evidence: This is speculation about an alternative mechanism.

claim: In addition to its actin polymerizing function, FMNL1 has also been implicated in actin bundling and severing activities.
source: In addition to its actin polymerizing function, FMNL1 has also been implicated in actin bundling and severing activities (Harris et al., 2004; Harris et al., 2006) and could remodel actin networks in various ways to promote TEM.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Harris et al., 2004; Harris et al., 2006.

claim: FMNL1 could remodel actin networks in various ways to promote TEM.
source: In addition to its actin polymerizing function, FMNL1 has also been implicated in actin bundling and severing activities (Harris et al., 2004; Harris et al., 2006) and could remodel actin networks in various ways to promote TEM.
evidence: This is speculation about potential mechanisms of FMNL1 action.

claim: Previous investigations of mDia1 observed defects in T cell development and trafficking to secondary lymphoid organs.
source: Previous investigations of mDia1, the other highly-expressed formin in T cells, observed defects in T cell development and trafficking to secondary lymphoid organs (Sakata et al., 2007; Eisenmann et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Sakata et al., 2007; Eisenmann et al., 2007.

claim: In FMNL1-deficient mice, normal populations of both developmental and mature T cells were observed and a selective requirement for FMNL1 extravasation through restrictive endothelial barriers and trafficking to inflamed tissues was identified.
source: In contrast, in FMNL1-deficient mice we observed normal populations of both developmental and mature T cells and identified a selective requirement for FMNL1 extravasation through restrictive endothelial barriers and trafficking to inflamed tissues.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from Figures 1, 2, and 3.

claim: Prior reports indicate that loss of mDia1 impairs chemotaxis even through non-restrictive barriers.
source: Furthermore, while prior reports indicate that loss of mDia1 impairs chemotaxis even through non-restrictive barriers (Thompson et al., 2018; Sakata et al., 2007), we observed that FMNL1 was selectively required for chemotaxis through narrow pores.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Thompson et al., 2018; Sakata et al., 2007.

claim: FMNL1 was selectively required for chemotaxis through narrow pores.
source: Furthermore, while prior reports indicate that loss of mDia1 impairs chemotaxis even through non-restrictive barriers (Thompson et al., 2018; Sakata et al., 2007), we observed that FMNL1 was selectively required for chemotaxis through narrow pores.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 6 showing pore size-dependent migration defects.

claim: These findings suggest a distinct and specific role for FMNL1 in mediating nuclear transmigration through restrictive endothelial barriers compared to a more general role for mDia1 in T cell motility.
source: Together these findings suggest a distinct and specific role for FMNL1 in mediating nuclear transmigration through restrictive endothelial barriers compared to a more general role for mDia1 in T cell motility.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the comparison of FMNL1 and mDia1 functions.

claim: The use of FMNL1 by T cells to promote transmigration of the nucleus may represent a unique mechanism compared to those employed by other immune cell types.
source: The use of FMNL1 by T cells to promote transmigration of the nucleus may represent a unique mechanism compared to those employed by other immune cell types.
evidence: This is speculation based on comparison with other cell types.

claim: Dendritic cells have been suggested to use actin polymerization by Arp2/3, instead of by formins, to facilitate nuclear deformation when migrating through restrictive environments.
source: For example, dendritic cells have been suggested to use actin polymerization by Arp2/3, instead of by formins, to facilitate nuclear deformation when migrating through restrictive environments (Thiam et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Thiam et al., 2016.

claim: Nuclear flexibility may dictate the requirement for actin mediated nuclear manipulation.
source: Nuclear flexibility may also dictate the requirement for actin mediated nuclear manipulation.
evidence: This is a general statement about the relationship between nuclear flexibility and actin-mediated mechanisms.

claim: It has been reported that neutrophils, which have multi-lobed deformable nuclei, or cells with induced nuclear flexibility do not display perinuclear actin accumulation when encountering restrictive spaces, while cells with rigid nuclei do.
source: It has been reported that neutrophils, which have multi-lobed deformable nuclei, or cells with induced nuclear flexibility do not display perinuclear actin accumulation when encountering restrictive spaces, while cells with rigid nuclei do (Thiam et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Thiam et al., 2016.

claim: Consistent with the literature, FMNL1 was dispensable for neutrophil migration through narrow pores, while in activated T cells, varying the level of FMNL1 expression strongly correlated with narrow pore transmigration.
source: Consistent with this literature, we observed that FMNL1 was dispensable for neutrophil migration through narrow pores, while in activated T cells, varying the level of FMNL1 expression strongly correlated with narrow pore transmigration.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figures 6B and 6F.

claim: After activation, the nuclear volume of T cells increases but still maintains a rigid ovoid structure in contrast to the flexible segmented nuclear structure of neutrophils.
source: After activation, the nuclear volume of T cells increases but still maintains a rigid ovoid structure in contrast to the flexible segmented nuclear structure of neutrophils (Gupta et al., 2012; Friedl et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gupta et al., 2012; Friedl et al., 2011.

claim: Similar to neutrophils, effector T cells must rapidly migrate into tissues to execute their functions.
source: However, similar to neutrophils, effector T cells must rapidly migrate into tissues to execute their functions (Masopust and Schenkel, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Masopust and Schenkel, 2013.

claim: FMNL1-driven perinuclear actin polymerization in activated T cells compensates for their increased nuclear size and rigidity by facilitating nuclear migration through constricted environments such as the restrictive endothelial barriers of non-lymphoid tissues.
source: Thus, we propose that FMNL1-driven perinuclear actin polymerization in activated T cells compensates for their increased nuclear size and rigidity by facilitating nuclear migration through constricted environments such as the restrictive endothelial barriers of non-lymphoid tissues.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the data showing FMNL1-dependent perinuclear actin polymerization and nuclear transmigration.

claim: Observations of T cell induced EAE and type 1 diabetes models suggest that reduced trafficking by FMNL1-deficient T cells to sites of inflammation plays a role in impairing the induction of autoimmune disease.
source: Our observations of T cell induced EAE and type 1 diabetes models suggest that reduced trafficking by FMNL1-deficient T cells to sites of inflammation plays a role in impairing the induction of autoimmune disease.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the trafficking and disease data in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: A partial but significant inhibition of trafficking was observed, while complete disease protection was observed in a subset of mice in both disease phenotypes.
source: While we observed a partial but significant inhibition of trafficking, we observed complete disease protection in a subset of mice in both disease phenotypes.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from Figures 2 and 3.

claim: The differences between trafficking inhibition and disease protection may be due to the fact that in the activated T cell transfer disease models, no prior immune infiltration has occurred, and thus, the vascular endothelial barriers are much more impermissive compared to the trafficking models where inflammation and immune cell recruitment is ongoing.
source: The differences between these findings may be due to the fact that in the activated T cell transfer disease models, no prior immune infiltration has occurred, and thus, the vascular endothelial barriers are much more impermissive compared to the trafficking models where inflammation and immune cell recruitment is ongoing.
evidence: This is speculation about the reason for the difference between trafficking and disease outcomes.

claim: There may be a threshold effect whereby trafficking is reduced such that the number of FMNL1-deficient T cells capable of entering the tissue are not sufficient to induce disease.
source: Furthermore, there may be a threshold effect whereby trafficking is reduced such that the number of FMNL1-deficient T cells capable of entering the tissue are not sufficient to induce disease.
evidence: This is speculation about a potential threshold effect.

claim: In the disease contexts examined, FMNL1 may have additional roles within the disease site or might impact migration within restrictive tissue parenchyma.
source: While, in this report, we have examined the function of FMNL1 in T cell TEM, it is also possible that, in these disease contexts, FMNL1 may have additional roles within the disease site or might impact migration within restrictive tissue parenchyma.
evidence: This is speculation about potential additional roles of FMNL1.

claim: It has been previously reported that knockdown of FMNL1 slightly impaired human CD8 T cell killing in vitro.
source: It has been previously reported that knockdown of FMNL1 slightly impaired human CD8 T cell killing in vitro (Gomez et al., 2007), thus FMNL1 deficiency may also play a role in OT-I T cell effector function in the RIP-mOVA model.

claim: FMNL1 deficiency may play a role in OT-I T cell effector function in the RIP-mOVA model.
source: It has been previously reported that knockdown of FMNL1 slightly impaired human CD8 T cell killing in vitro (Gomez et al., 2007), thus FMNL1 deficiency may also play a role in OT-I T cell effector function in the RIP-mOVA model.
evidence: This is speculation based on previous findings.

claim: Future study of FMNL1 function in T cells within tissues may identify additional mechanisms by which FMNL1 regulates T cell behavior.
source: Future study of FMNL1 function in T cells within tissues may identify additional mechanisms by which FMNL1 regulates T cell behavior.
evidence: This is a statement about future research directions.

claim: Inhibition of T cell trafficking has shown therapeutic promise in the treatment of autoimmune and inflammatory disease.
source: Inhibition of T cell trafficking has shown therapeutic promise in the treatment of autoimmune and inflammatory disease (Luster et al., 2005; Engelhardt and Kappos, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Luster et al., 2005; Engelhardt and Kappos, 2008.

claim: Observations that FMNL1 deficiency in T cells impairs their ability to traffic to autoimmune inflammatory sites and induce autoimmune disease in both EAE and type 1 diabetes suggest that FMNL1 may be a potential therapeutic target for autoimmune disease treatment.
source: Our observations that FMNL1 deficiency in T cells impairs their ability to traffic to autoimmune inflammatory sites and induce autoimmune disease in both EAE and type 1 diabetes suggest that FMNL1 may be a potential therapeutic target for autoimmune disease treatment.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the disease data suggesting therapeutic potential.

claim: As immune cell development and homeostatic trafficking appear unaltered by global FMNL1 deficiency, targeting of FMNL1 may offer the possibility of selectively impairing activated T cell trafficking to specific tissue sites while leaving systemic immune surveillance intact.
source: As immune cell development and homeostatic trafficking appear unaltered by global FMNL1 deficiency, targeting of FMNL1 may offer the possibility of selectively impairing activated T cell trafficking to specific tissue sites while leaving systemic immune surveillance intact.
evidence: This is speculation about therapeutic potential based on the selective effects of FMNL1 deficiency.

claim: A recent report has suggested that selectively inhibiting activated T cell trafficking may be particularly beneficial in the context of graft-versus-host disease.
source: A recent report has suggested that selectively inhibiting activated T cell trafficking may be particularly beneficial in the context of graft-versus-host disease (Huang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Huang et al., 2015.

claim: Previously studied cytoskeletal effectors of T cell migration, such as Arp2/3, mDia1, MyoIIA and Ena/Vasp proteins are expressed in most tissues and cell types.
source: While previously studied cytoskeletal effectors of T cell migration, such as Arp2/3, mDia1, MyoIIA and Ena/Vasp proteins are expressed in most tissues and cell types, FMNL1 expression is largely restricted to hematopoietic cells (Yayoshi-Yamamoto et al., 2000; Gardberg et al., 2014; Yue et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the expression patterns of cytoskeletal proteins.

claim: The restricted expression of FMNL1 to hematopoietic cells may offer the possibility of a more targeted approach to therapeutically alter cytoskeletal function in immune cells.
source: This expression profile may offer the possibility of a more targeted approach to therapeutically alter cytoskeletal function in immune cells.
evidence: This is speculation about therapeutic potential based on FMNL1's restricted expression.

claim: The observations have uncovered a new mechanism that promotes lymphocyte nucleus passage through constrictive environments.
source: In conclusion, our observations have uncovered a new mechanism that promotes lymphocyte nucleus passage through constrictive environments.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main finding.

source: This process of FMNL1-dependent nucleus transmigration is key for the extravasation of effector T cells through the restrictive vascular endothelial barriers present in non-lymphoid tissues.

source: Furthermore, FMNL1 deficiency in T cells impairs their ability to induce autoimmune disease, suggesting that targeting of FMNL1 may be therapeutically beneficial.

source: Thus, our observation that FMNL1-deficient T cells are impaired in transmigration of their nuclei across endothelial barriers is consistent with our finding that FMNL1-deficient T cells are impaired in transmigrating through 3 μm but not 5 μm transwell pores.

claim: Neutrophils express FMNL1 at similar levels to T cells.
source: Neutrophils also express FMNL1 at similar levels to T cells (Ericson et al., 2014) but are characterized by a multi-lobed, more flexible, nuclear structure (Feng et al., 1998; Mackarel et al., 1999; Yadav et al., 2018).

claim: Neutrophils are characterized by a multi-lobed, more flexible, nuclear structure.

evidence: This is supported by citations to Feng et al., 1998; Mackarel et al., 1999; Yadav et al., 2018.

source: These findings suggest that in cell types with more flexible nuclei, the need for FMNL1 in transmigrating through restrictive openings is reduced.
